Arjuna: O Krishna, seeing my own kinsmen assembled here eager for battle, my limbs fail and my mouth is parched.
My body trembles, my hair stands on end; the Gandiva slips from my hand, and my skin burns.
I am unable to stand steady, and my mind seems to whirl. I see only evil omens, O Keshava. I do not foresee any good in killing my own people in battle.
I desire neither victory nor kingdom nor pleasures. Of what use to us are kingdom, enjoyments, or even life itself?

Those for whose sake we desire kingdom, pleasures, and happiness—teachers, fathers, sons, grandfathers, maternal uncles, fathers-in-law, grandsons, brothers-in-law, and other relatives—stand here in battle, ready to renounce their lives and wealth.
O Madhusudana, even if they kill me, I do not wish to kill them—not even for sovereignty over the three worlds, how much less for this earth.
O Janardana, what joy shall we have in killing the sons of Dhritarashtra? Sin alone will cling to us if we slay these aggressors.
Therefore, it is not proper for us to kill our own kinsmen. How can we be happy after killing our own people?

Though they, with minds overpowered by greed, see no evil in the destruction of family and no sin in hostility to friends, why should we not turn away from this sin, knowing the evil of destroying a family?
With the destruction of family, ancient family traditions perish; when tradition is lost, irreligion overwhelms the family.
When irreligion prevails, the women of the family become corrupted; and when women are corrupted, O descendant of Vrishni, there arises intermixture of castes.
This intermixture leads the destroyers of the family to hell, for their forefathers fall, deprived of offerings of food and water.
By these evils of those who destroy family traditions, the eternal customs of caste and family are ruined.
We have heard, O Krishna, that men whose family traditions are destroyed dwell in hell for an indefinite period.
Alas! We are resolved to commit a great sin, driven by greed for royal pleasure, in seeking to kill our own kinsmen.
It would be better for me if the sons of Dhritarashtra, armed with weapons, were to kill me unresisting and unarmed on the battlefield.

Krishna: From where has this dejection come upon you at this critical moment, Arjuna? It is unworthy of a noble person; it leads neither to heaven nor to honor.
Do not yield to this weakness, O Partha. It does not befit you. Cast off this petty faint-heartedness and arise, O scorcher of enemies.

Arjuna: O Madhusudana, how shall I fight with arrows in battle against Bhishma and Drona, who are worthy of reverence?
It is better to live by begging in this world than to slay these noble elders. Having killed them, even worldly enjoyments would be stained with blood.
We do not know which is better—fighting or not fighting. Nor do we know whether we shall conquer them or they will conquer us.
My nature is overcome by pity; my mind is confused regarding duty. I ask You—tell me decisively what is good for me. I am Your disciple; I have taken refuge in You.
I see no means of removing this sorrow that dries up my senses, even if I obtain an unrivaled kingdom on earth or sovereignty over the gods.

Krishna: You grieve for those who should not be grieved for, yet you speak words of wisdom. The wise grieve neither for the living nor for the dead.
Never was there a time when I did not exist, nor you, nor these kings; nor shall any of us cease to exist in the future.
Just as the embodied soul passes in this body through childhood, youth, and old age, so it passes into another body. The wise are not deluded by this.
The contacts of the senses with their objects give rise to cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and are impermanent; endure them, O Bharata.
That person whom these do not disturb, who is the same in pleasure and pain, is fit for immortality.
The unreal has no existence; the real never ceases to be. The truth of both has been seen by the seers of truth.
Know that to be indestructible by which this entire universe is pervaded. None can destroy the imperishable.
These bodies are perishable; the soul within is imperishable, eternal, and immeasurable. Therefore, fight, O Arjuna.
He who thinks the soul kills and he who thinks it is killed—both are ignorant. The soul neither kills nor is killed.
The soul is never born, nor does it die. Having once existed, it never ceases to be. It is unborn, eternal, everlasting, and ancient. It is not slain when the body is slain.
Just as a person discards worn-out garments and puts on new ones, so the soul discards worn-out bodies and enters new ones.
Weapons do not cut it, fire does not burn it, water does not wet it, and wind does not dry it.
This soul is uncuttable, unburnable, unwettable, and undryable. It is eternal, all-pervading, stable, immovable, and everlasting.
